This website is produced by the M2 MODE student during year 2025-2026 as part of their assignment in the Online Collaborative Resources course.

They were asked to produce collaboratively different illustrations on ecological data for different statistical and mathematical models.

Just click on one of the three menus on top right side of this page to visit their work. They have used up to data version control workflows to produce this website using git Github, Pull Request, Code review. A set of good practices to help them producible research in the futur.

The website is fully generated using Continuous Integration (CI) based on Github Action.

## Evaluation

### Quiz — October 7 (coeff 2)
- Format: in class, with no doc (multiple choice and open questions), 30 mn durations.
- Covers: Quarto and Git (basic quarto command understanding and question on process development using git)

### Final Assignment (coeff 3)

**Quarto part**
- Clear presentation of the dataset, including a basic descriptive analysis (graphs and/or tables)
- Numbered equations, figures, and/or tables (generated and included), with in-text references to each
- A shared bibliography file (`.bib`) used to cite relevant references, `OCR_TP.bib` 
- Expected folder structure: 
  - dataset should be stored in `data/` or accessible,
  - figures hould be stored in figures 
  - one qmd file per group

**Git part**
- Clear, meaningful commit messages
- Clear commit tree showing the development process
- Use a branch for each new feature or aspect of the work
- Avoid merge commits — keep history as linear and clean as possible
- **Do not merge directly into `main`** — use Pull Requests (use the **rebase** option when merging)
- Minimum commit frequency: *[e.g. regular commits throughout the project, not a single commit at the deadline]*
- CI must pass on the final PR/commit before submission is considered complete

## Collaboration Guidelines

Several files are shared among groups — be careful when modifying them. **Do not overwrite or destroy someone else's work.**

- Always `pull`/`fetch` before starting work each session
- If you hit a merge conflict, resolve it carefully and check with your group before force-pushing; contact the instructor if unsure
- The `main` branch is protected — all changes go through a reviewed PR
- Remember to `.gitignore` generated files (rendered output, virtual environments, cache files, etc.) — don't commit them

## Technical Notes

- If using RStudio's visual editor, be aware it can produce messy diffs on `.qmd` files — prefer the source editor when committing, or review your diff carefully before committing
- Keep the repository structure consistent with what your group agreed on at the start of the project

### Grading breakdown

**Quarto part — 30 points (group grade)**

| Criterion | Points |
|---|---|
| Clear presentation of the dataset + descriptive analysis (graphs/tables) | 10 |
| Numbered equations, figures and/or tables, generated, with in-text references | 8 |
| Shared bibliography file, used correctly (citations + rendering) | 6 |
| Overall document quality (clarity, structure, readability, clean rendering) | 6 |

**Git part — 70 points**

| Criterion | Level | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Clear, informative commit messages | Individual | 10 |
| Readable commit tree within one's own branch | Group | 10 |
| Coherence/impact of the history at PR/merge time into `main` | Group | 10 |
| Use of branches (one per feature/aspect) | Individual | 10 |
| Clean history — no unnecessary merge commits | Group | 10 |
| Correct PR usage (no direct merge into `main`), rebase used | Group | 10 |
| Regularity of commits throughout the project | Individual | 10 |

**Penalties**
- **-10 points for the group** if another group's work is destroyed/overwritten at merge time
- **-10 points for the group** if the website is no longer functional after a PR
